agree.reason: A wary reader who has quit three services would find the honest A1C framing and the six-month retention figure reassuring, but the page never answers their real worry about getting bored and quitting again, and it says nothing about the no-contract terms or the call with the dietitian.

honest.reason: The page drops the requested 'will lower your A1C' promise, reports 10 down, 3 the same and 1 up out of 14 self-selected customers, and says medication changes weren't tracked; the only soft spot is the unsupported claim that the meals 'taste good'.

works_the_facts.reason: The figures are reported accurately but barely worked: 37 of 88 isn't turned into roughly 42% staying past six months, the full plan isn't given as about $12.90 per meal, and the trial isn't shown as a cheaper per-meal test.

right_comparison.reason: The alternative is a generic picture of counting carbs and reading labels, not the reader's actual history of starting and dropping apps and services, which the retention data could have answered directly.

qualification.reason: The hedges are concrete and checkable: 14 self-selected customers, three months, medication not accounted for, and a clear no-promise statement, though none ties the result to a consequence.

objections.reason: The medication-and-doctor objection is handled well, but the main objections of variety, commitment and getting stuck are left open even though the facts covered them (meal swaps from 6 choices, a 4-week menu cycle, no contract with skip or cancel any time, and a 15-minute call).

fit.reason: It is a sales page close to the 400-word target with a clear order button, but [Service Name], [Your Name] and [Metro Area] are left as placeholders, and the Thursday-noon order cutoff and 25-mile delivery radius are missing.
